content: Afrotheria is a taxonomic clade of mammals classified at the rank of superorder or cohort. This group includes a diverse array of species such as golden moles, elephant shrews, tenrecs, aardvarks, hyraxes, elephants, and manatees. The evolutionary relationships within Afrotheria have been proposed primarily based on molecular and DNA analyses. Since the 1990s, genetic studies have identified Afrotheria as one of the four major groups within the infraclass Eutheria, which encompasses placental mammals. The other three groups are Xenarthra, Laurasiatheria, and Euarchontoglires (also known as Supraprimates). However, the precise evolutionary relationships among these four cohorts remain a topic of debate. One hypothesis suggests that Afrotheria diverged from the other three groups approximately 105 million years ago, coinciding with the geographic isolation of the African continent from other major landmasses. The term Afrotheria is derived from the Greek roots Afro(referring to Africa) and -theria (meaning animal). Genetic and fossil evidence indicates that Xenarthra, which includes anteaters, sloths, and armadillos, likely evolved in South America and diverged from the remaining two groups at a later time. Laurasiatheria and Euarchontoglires are thought to be more closely related to each other than to Afrotheria or Xenarthra, and they are often grouped together under the taxon Boreoeutheria. Some researchers consider these classifications, based on recent comparative DNA analyses, to be preliminary or controversial, as they often conflict with earlier groupings of mammalian relationships that were based on morphological characteristics. For instance, the traditional order Insectivora, which included many genera and species of small, insect-eating mammals, is now understood to consist of distantly related species. Their similar anatomy and behaviors are now thought to result from convergent evolution rather than close evolutionary relationships. Similarly, the distinctive morphological traits of Xenarthra previously led taxonomists to classify all other eutherian mammals into the taxon Epitheria, with Xenarthra as the most distantly related group. Another reconstruction places Xenarthra and Afrotheria together within the clade Atlantogenata, as a sister clade to Boreoeutheria. Many members of Afrotheria are currently at high risk of extinction. If the grouping is accurate, the loss of these species would represent a significant reduction in genetic and evolutionary diversity. The Afrotheria Specialist Group has noted that Afrotheria, as currently reconstructed, includes nearly one-third of all mammalian orders found in Africa and Madagascar, yet it comprises only 75 species out of more than 1,200 mammalian species in these regions. While most extant Afrotherian species are found in Africa, some, such as the Indian elephant and the three species of manatees, are found elsewhere. Many of these species are also endangered. Afrotheria is a division of the infraclass Eutheria (placental mammals) and includes six extant orders of mammals. These are: 1. Order Afrosoricida: Suborder Chrysochloridea: Golden moles (21 species). Suborder Tenrecomorpha: Tenrecs and otter shrews (32 species). 2. Order Macroscelidea: Elephant shrews or sengis (15 species). 3. Order Tubulidentata: Aardvark (1 species). 4. Clade Paenungulata: Order Hyracoidea: Hyraxes (4–6 species, depending on subspecies classification). Order Proboscidea: Elephants (3 species). Order Sirenia: Manatees (3 species), dugong (1 species), and several extinct species of sea cows. 5. Extinct Orders: Order Embrithopoda: Extinct. Order Desmostylia: Extinct. Afrotheria is believed to have originated in Africa during a period when the continent was geographically isolated from other landmasses. The only externally visible common characteristic among Afrotherians is the presence of a movable snout, although there is no definitive evidence that this feature is homologous across all members of the group. The fossil record presents challenges to the idea of Afrotherians as an exclusively African clade, as the earliest fossil evidence for African ungulates and elephant shrews has been found outside Africa. Afrotherians are part of the proposed clade Atlantogenata. However, the monophyly of Afrotheria is not universally accepted. Morphological evidence places elephants and their relatives as true ungulates, and this may also apply to aardvarks and elephant shrews, though not to tenrecs and golden moles. Elephant shrews may even be more closely related to gnawing mammals within Glires. A mammal known from Madagascar, Plesioryctopus, has uncertain affinities but may also be an ungulate, possibly related to the mainland aardvark. Some morphological evidence supports the affinity of tenrecs and golden moles to other Lipotyphlan insectivores, particularly the Solenodon found in the Caribbean region. This interpretation aligns with more traditional views of Tenrecomorph relationships.
